description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

items.title: Sandworm and Qilin are inside Cisco firewall management: a critical auth bypass, exploited since August
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 — a critical authentication bypass in Secure Firewall Management Center, patched back in March — has been exploited since August. Crafted HTTP requests reach a process created at boot and hand an unauthenticated attacker root on the appliance that configures your firewalls. Cisco Talos attributes three activity clusters: one deploying a web shell to harvest credentials, one tied to the Russian state group Sandworm delivering Cyclops Blink, and one linked to Qilin ransomware staging encryption target lists. CISA added the flaw to KEV with a federal remediation deadline of 12 September, which has now passed. For OT defenders the significance is not the firewall — it is the management plane above it. Whoever holds FMC holds the rule set separating enterprise from plant, and can rewrite it without touching a single controller.

items.title: An industrial automation vendor lost its SCADA/HMI source code — to a public proof-of-concept weaponised within days
items.content_text: Acronis Threat Research Unit published findings on 15 September describing a PRC-linked, Chinese-speaking actor it tracks as Red Heron, which turned a public proof-of-concept for a critical Gitea remote code execution flaw (CVE-2026-60004) into an automated mass-exploitation campaign within days of the code appearing. The operators scanned 1,386 internet-facing Gitea instances across seven countries and kept a separate list of 477 Taiwan-based systems, classified by target type: defence, energy, aerospace, telecommunications, government, research and election or voting systems. Acronis confirmed compromises at eleven organisations in Canada, the United States, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka. The heaviest loss was a Taiwanese industrial automation company, from which the operators pulled hundreds of repositories including a SCADA/HMI product, surveillance and monitoring software, IoT platform integrations and a network sniffer.

items.title: The water campaign, quantified: CISA counts 100-plus internet-exposed systems hit, with controller logic and alarms altered
items.content_text: CISA has put a figure on July’s campaign against US water utilities: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, with reporting placing targeting across at least a dozen. Some degraded operations — lost pressure, flooding, plants run by hand — though supply was not widely interrupted, and in several intrusions actors altered controllers to disable shutdown processes and alarms, letting unsafe conditions develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. It stays on the page five weeks on because of the admission behind the number: the exposure that carried it was in nobody’s asset register.

items.title: The water campaign was not the whole campaign — telecoms and energy control systems are now being probed, and there is a $10 million bounty on the man said to run it
items.content_text: Two developments this week moved the summer’s dominant OT story past the water sector. NBC News reported on 2 September, citing four people with access to government and industry threat information, that Iran-linked operators have spent recent weeks probing internet-facing automated control systems at telecommunications and energy providers as well as water utilities — and that those attempts have so far been unsuccessful. A day later the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme posted a reward of up to $10 million for information identifying or locating Amir Yaryab, named as head of the cyber operations division of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and accused of directing groups including the CyberAv3ngers persona against US critical infrastructure. Separately, a Telegram channel presenting itself as a voice for Iranian cyber operations has threatened action against US energy, water and telecommunications, without evidence of any successful operation. The signal for defenders is the change of aim, not a new capability: the same tradecraft that found exposed water PLCs in July is now being pointed at neighbouring sectors that run the same internet-facing gear.

items.title: A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
items.content_text: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable.

items.title: A device manufacturer could not ship for a fortnight — and the plant floor was never touched
items.content_text: Boston Scientific identified a cybersecurity incident on 25 August 2026 that took down on-premises IT systems across its global operations, disclosed it the following day, and then spent roughly two weeks unable to process or ship customer orders. The company said on 9 September that manufacturing, order fulfilment and shipping were fully restored and that product was moving through distribution at or above normal levels while backlogs cleared. Cloud-hosted systems were not affected, no unauthorised activity was found after 25 August, and CrowdStrike was engaged for the response. A separate knock-on effect blocked remote activation of communicators for newly implanted cardiac devices and pairing for new insertable monitors; that was declared resolved on 8 September, and devices already enrolled in remote monitoring continued to function throughout. No compromise of ICS, PLC or process-control systems has been reported. The reason this belongs on an OT page is the shape of the outage rather than its cause: the machines kept running and the company still could not get product out of the door.

items.title: A municipal utility lost its whole back office and kept the lights on — the separation held, and it is worth reading why
items.content_text: Stadtwerke Landsberg am Lech, the Bavarian municipal utility that supplies electricity, water, wastewater, district heating and fibre to a town of roughly 30,000, disclosed a criminal cyberattack that encrypted its central IT systems on 1 September 2026. File servers, the ERP database and administrative server clusters were either encrypted or pre-emptively shut down; corporate email and VoIP telephony were cut from external networks, leaving customers unable to reach the utility by phone or email for days. The utility stated that the systems controlling electricity, water and heat supply were not affected and continued to run normally. It disconnected the affected environment from the internet, stood up a crisis team and brought in external responders; by 7 September enough administrative capability was restored to resume customer service and contract processing. No group has claimed the attack and the utility has not said whether an extortion demand was made. It cannot yet rule out theft of customer names, addresses, contact details and bank data.

items.title: Four ways to knock a Siemens edge gateway off the PROFINET segment — and blind SCADA while you do it
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published research on 15 September detailing four memory-corruption flaws in the PROFINET Discovery and basic Configuration Protocol implementation on the Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 industrial PC, found using emulation-driven snapshot fuzzing with the Unicorn CPU emulator and AFL++. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2025-40575 through CVE-2025-40578 — an uninitialised-value issue, a NULL pointer dereference and two out-of-bounds reads — each carrying a CVSS 4.0 score of 5.3, and affect firmware up to V4.0 HF0. The DCP daemon runs as root, requires no authentication and is bound to all three device interfaces, so an attacker already on the same Layer 2 segment can crash it with crafted Ethernet frames. Siemens has shipped fixed firmware.

items.title: Five agencies say the S7 family is being actively hunted — and that the exploit scripts are being written with AI
items.content_text: The joint advisory published on 19 August is the primary-source anchor under this edition’s AI research. The NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE and EPA report threat actors actively working against Siemens S7 controllers that are internet-exposed or poorly segmented, spanning the S7‑200, ‑300, ‑400, ‑1200 and ‑1500 lines, and name Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater, Chemical, Food and Agriculture and Commercial Facilities as the most affected sectors. What makes it notable is the method: the agencies describe AI‑generated reconnaissance and exploitation scripts built around the open-source python‑snap7 library and disguised to look like legitimate OT monitoring tooling. Two familiar conditions do the enabling — internet exposure through weak segmentation, and default or weak credentials. The protocol expertise that used to gate ICS exploit development is no longer the barrier.

items.title: A frontier model ported a working PLC exploit to a second controller in eight hours — then bricked it
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published the result of a deliberately awkward experiment: point a frontier AI model at real industrial hardware and see how far it gets. Starting from the team’s own remote code execution exploit for a WAGO 750-852, built on CVE-2021-31886 — a pre-authentication overflow in the Nucleus FTP server — they asked Claude to port it to the related 750-831, giving the model a terminal, Ghidra and the physical device. It worked, but not cleanly. The first model tried failed to trace the vulnerable function; a stronger model eventually worked out why the injected shellcode was being wiped before it could run, and once past that it produced two working payloads in twelve minutes. Total cost of the final stage: over eight hours and more than $500 in API charges. A follow-up attempt at a command-and-control implant wrote to flash and permanently bricked the PLC.

items.title: Six agencies publish the 17 ways attackers take Active Directory — which is how most of them reach a control network
items.content_text: On 15 September 2026, CISA, the NSA, Australia’s ASD, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, New Zealand’s NCSC and the UK’s NCSC jointly published guidance describing seventeen techniques the agencies observe being used against Microsoft Active Directory, with detection and mitigation advice for each. It spans Active Directory Domain Services, Certificate Services and Federation Services, and covers credential theft, Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting, Kerberos ticket forgery, directory-replication abuse, certificate-template abuse, privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence and hybrid-identity compromise. This is an enterprise-identity publication rather than an ICS one, which is precisely why it belongs here: in the great majority of documented OT intrusions the adversary does not exploit a controller to get in — they take the domain first, then walk into engineering workstations, historians, HMIs and jump hosts holding valid credentials. Several of the seventeen work equally well against an OT domain that trusts, or is trusted by, the corporate one.

items.title: The hypervisor under your SCADA estate is now a ransomware target — and CISA said so at the weekend
items.content_text: CISA updated its KEV entry for CVE-2026-59310 over the weekend of 13–14 September to record that ransomware operators have joined the attacks on it. The flaw is a critical directory-traversal weakness in the vCenter Syslog service, patched by Broadcom on 29 July, which lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access run arbitrary code on the management server. DFIR firm QUIRSO reported over 361 compromised IP addresses in 47 countries two weeks after the fix, from an actor deploying a reverse-SSH tool for persistence; CISA added the CVE to KEV on 18 August with a three-day federal deadline. Shadowserver still sees more than 450 vCenter servers exposed to the internet. For OT this is not an IT story: the historian, HMI and engineering virtual machines on the other side of that hypervisor are the ones that stop.

items.title: An email is now a root shell: Cisco’s mail gateway is being exploited as a zero-day, and it takes no clicks at all
items.content_text: Cisco told customers on Monday that CVE-2026-76461, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in the email-parsing logic of AsyncOS, has been exploited in the wild as a zero-day. A remote, unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted message containing malicious SQL statements; insufficient validation in the parser executes them, ending in arbitrary operating-system commands as root on the appliance. No credentials, no user interaction, no one has to open anything. Both physical and virtual Secure Email Gateways are affected in any configuration; Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 17 September federal deadline. For OT programmes the uncomfortable part is second-order: this is the second Cisco appliance in a week under confirmed attack, and both sit upstream of the enterprise identity your plant network still trusts.

items.title: September’s ICS Patch Tuesday reaches the safety controller: a CVSS 9.2 authentication flaw in Schneider’s Modicon M580
items.content_text: Schneider Electric, Siemens and Aveva published their September advisories on 8 September, and the one that matters most sits inside a controller family run on safety duty. CVE-2026-3869, rated CVSS 9.2, is an authentication weakness in the Modicon M580 and M580 Safety ranges — the mid-tier PLC that runs a great many water, power and process plants, and the same hardware many sites rely on for safety functions. Schneider also fixed high-severity defects in PowerLogic T300 and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, and finally shipped Modicon MC80 patches for weaknesses first disclosed as far back as 2019. Siemens added four critical advisories, including the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay. CISA followed on 10 September with ICSA-26-253-01, the formal advisory for the Aveva Pipeline Integrity Monitor flaws, which is the only new ICS advisory it published in the last two days. Nothing here is exploited. What makes it consequential is where it lands: on the devices whose failure mode is physical, not informational — and on a patch clock measured in validated outages rather than days.

items.title: The firewall in front of your plant DMZ can be taken with one malformed XML request — root, no credentials
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks is telling customers to treat CVE-2026-0310 with its highest remediation urgency. A buffer overflow in how PAN-OS parses XML lets an unauthenticated attacker with network reach to an affected interface write outside the buffer — a denial of service on VM-Series, and arbitrary code as root on PA-Series hardware. Panorama is in scope too. The vendor scores it CVSS v4 9.2; the threat-adjusted CVSS-BT score sits at 7.2 because no exploitation has been observed yet. That gap is the whole planning question. For OT programmes the relevant detail is where these boxes sit: PA-Series hardware is what most sizeable operators use to enforce the Purdue boundary, and Panorama is the console that writes those rules across the estate. Root on the enforcement point is not an IT problem.

items.title: The remote-support client your integrator installed can now push and run files on your machine without asking — and it is in KEV
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 September with a 14 September federal deadline. The flaw sits in the ConnectWise ScreenConnect client — improper privilege management combined with a missing authorisation check — and it lets files be transferred to and executed on a connected machine through an already-active remote session, without authorisation and without the host confirmation prompt that operators are trained to watch for. CVSS is 9.9. ConnectWise says servers are not affected; the fix is client version 26.6.5. Huntress documented three unrelated incidents in which rogue ScreenConnect installations pushed a malicious VBScript payload to newly connected systems, which is the detail that matters: the abuse path runs from the support platform outward to the endpoint, in the direction integrators and OEMs normally use to reach a plant.

items.title: The other remote-access box just went live: public exploit code for a NetScaler auth bypass, and attacks the same week
items.content_text: Citrix patched CVE-2026-19490 on 19 August — an authentication bypass, CVSS 9.3, in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy) or as an AAA virtual server, with SAML configurations among those affected. For a fortnight it stayed theoretical. Then public exploit code appeared in early September, and on 3 September sensor operators began recording bypass attempts from multiple source addresses across four countries, with reporting on 4 September confirming attackers had turned to the flaw in the wild. NetScaler is not an OT product, but it is very often the thing an engineer authenticates through before reaching a jump host, a historian or a vendor session — which makes an unauthenticated bypass on it a route to the plant, not merely to the corporate estate.

items.title: CERT Polska confirms attackers are taking full control of internet-facing MikroTik routers — the box that quietly backhauls half the remote sites in your fleet
items.content_text: CERT Polska disclosed six RouterOS vulnerabilities on 5 September and confirmed that two of them are already being chained in live attacks. The chain, named MikroTrick, pairs CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2) — RouterOS validated only part of an SSH RSA public key, so an attacker who knows a username and the key’s public modulus can forge a key and log in without the private half — with CVE-2026-86060 (CVSS 9.2), a username-parsing flaw that hands the resulting session full administrative rights. Together they give unauthenticated device takeover wherever SSH answers from the internet. A third flaw, CVE-2026-67277 (CVSS 8.8), leaks kernel memory or reboots the device through the unauthenticated bandwidth-test service. MikroTik patched on 3 September in 6.49.21, 7.23.4, 7.24.2 and 7.25beta3. CERT Polska says confirmed compromises trace to 82.192.72.4 and run back to at least 2 September. This matters in OT because RouterOS is the cheap, ubiquitous router behind remote pump stations, substations, wellheads, irrigation skids and contractor-built field cabinets — equipment that is frequently outside the OT asset register and reachable from the internet by design.

items.title: A fourth boundary box in a fortnight: a CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the platform your outsourced IT uses to reach every machine you own
items.content_text: N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218 on 6 September and rated it CVSS 10.0 — an unauthenticated attacker can execute code on an internet-exposed N-central server, in a low-complexity attack requiring no credentials and no user interaction. The fix is N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4, build 2026.3.1.14, and reporting notes it is the fourth N-central hotfix in roughly five weeks. Huntress reported a compromised production environment but could not establish which of the disclosed flaws was used, and flagged this one as a possible zero-day alongside two high-severity issues; N-able’s own notice describes exploitation observed in the wild. The Shadowserver Foundation tracks close to 1,500 internet-exposed N-central servers, most in the United States and Europe. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform — an agent with system-level rights on every endpoint it manages. For industrial sites, the question is whether the managed service provider that patches your engineering workstations, historians and plant IT runs one, and whether their console is reachable from the internet.

items.title: CISA’s 1 September batch is five-sixths Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
items.content_text: CISA published eight ICS advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The set covers RSLinx Classic (ICSA-26-244-01), the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (-02), the Logix platform (-03), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). The RSLinx item is the one most sites will feel first: four flaws — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625 — let crafted Common Industrial Protocol traffic crash the communications service on version 4.50 and earlier, and it stays down until somebody restarts it by hand. RSLinx is the data path between controllers and the HMI, historian and engineering workstations, so a crash there is a visibility outage on a running process, not an IT inconvenience. The batch also carries an update to the Rockwell 1734 POINT I/O advisory (ICSA-26-202-09, Update A) and Update G to the long-running Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software advisory (ICSA-24-135-04). Rockwell’s own round-up, reported 2 September, puts the total above a dozen fixes and adds detail the CISA summaries do not: remote code execution in FactoryTalk Historian, privilege escalation in FactoryTalk Activation Manager and in the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool, arbitrary code execution through the ControlFLASH firmware utility, cross-site scripting plus a web-server denial of service in ArmorStart distributed motor controllers, and further denial-of-service issues in 1756-ENBT and in Logix controllers via a third-party component. One item needs care rather than alarm: Rockwell’s advisory for CVE-2026-9637, a high-severity denial of service in ControlLogix and CompactLogix, is flagged as exploited in its document header but listed as not exploited in the body, and CISA states it is not aware of exploitation — read it as a documentation inconsistency, not a live campaign, and patch it on its merits.

items.title: The clock has started: anyone selling a connected product into the EU now owes a 24-hour warning on exploited vulnerabilities
items.content_text: The EU Cyber Resilience Act entered its reporting phase on 11 September 2026. As of yesterday, manufacturers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting their products, with an early warning inside 24 hours and a fuller notification inside 72 hours. The scope reaches far past consumer IoT: PLCs, RTUs, drives, gateways, HMIs, protocol converters and the engineering software around them are products with digital elements, and the obligation follows the manufacturer regardless of where the affected device is installed. Legal analysts advise naming an owner now and building the assessment, escalation and customer-communication path in advance, coordinating it with existing NIS2 and GDPR duties rather than standing up a third parallel process.

items.title: FERC signs off on CIP-014-4 — a tighter, more consistent test for which substations count as critical
items.content_text: FERC issued an order on 10 September 2026 approving NERC Reliability Standard CIP-014-4, published in the Federal Register on 15 September. CIP-014 is the physical security standard for the bulk-power system, and this revision targets the part registered entities have found most contestable: how transmission stations, transmission substations and primary control centres are identified and assessed as critical to reliable operation. The revision pushes toward a more consistent, repeatable identification methodology across entities rather than adding a new control set. It is a physical-security standard, but OT security staff should not file it under someone else’s programme — the risk assessment that decides a station is critical is the same assessment that should be driving cyber scoping for the relays, RTUs, protection schemes and communications at that station, and at many utilities the two exercises are still run separately, years apart, on different criteria.

items.title: The Department of Energy picks three OT security tools to fund — and all three are aimed at the problem small utilities actually have
items.content_text: DOE has selected Frenos, Raptor Dynamix and Bastazo for funding under SENTRY (Securing ENergy Technology ResiliencY), the Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security and Emergency Response programme that pushes federally-backed research toward tools energy operators can deploy rather than papers they can read. The three selections cluster around the same bottleneck: not detecting attacks, but deciding what to do with a vulnerability list that nobody has the staff to work through. Frenos builds autonomous OT security assessment; Bastazo, which came out of DOE-funded research at the University of Arkansas, does AI-assisted vulnerability triage and remediation planning for OT, pitched explicitly at cutting a backlog down to the small fraction that carries real consequence. For asset owners the practical significance is not the vendors — it is that the federal funding thesis has shifted from visibility toward prioritisation and remediation, which is where most utility programmes are currently stuck.
